blocks.prompt: The Row of Singing Wood
blocks.text: A xylophone is a musical instrument made of wooden bars. The bars sit in a row from long to short. You play it by hitting the bars with two mallets. Each bar makes its own note. When you hit a long bar, it makes a low, deep note. When you hit a short bar, it makes a high, bright note. If you hit the bars in order, you can play a tune. The word xylophone comes from two old Greek words. One means wood and one means sound. So xylophone really means wood sound. That is a good name for a row of singing wood.

blocks.prompt: Wood That Makes Music
blocks.text: A xylophone is a row of wooden bars that you strike with mallets to make music. The bars are lined up from longest to shortest, a little like the keys on a piano. When you tap a bar, the whole bar shakes very fast, and that shaking pushes the air and makes a sound. Long bars shake slowly, so they make low notes. Short bars shake quickly, so they make high notes. That is why the bars are cut to different lengths. Under some xylophones you will find hollow tubes hanging below the bars. These tubes are called resonators. They catch the sound and make it louder and richer, so the note rings out instead of fading away. The name xylophone comes from ancient Greek. Xylon means wood and phone means sound, so the whole word means wood sound. People have built wooden instruments like this for a very long time. In parts of West Africa, players have used a wooden instrument called the balafon for hundreds of years, with dried gourds hung underneath to make the notes ring.

blocks.prompt: The Shape of a Note
blocks.text: A xylophone looks simple, but every part of it has a job. It is a row of wooden bars laid out from long to short, and you play it by striking the bars with hard mallets. Musicians group instruments in families, and the xylophone belongs to the family called idiophones. An idiophone makes its sound from the vibrating of its own solid body, with no strings and no stretched skin. When a mallet strikes a bar, the whole bar bends and springs back many times each second, and that rapid movement pushes the air into waves your ears hear as a note. The length of each bar sets its note. A long bar is heavy and springy, so it vibrates slowly and produces a low, deep tone. A short bar vibrates far more quickly and produces a high, bright tone. Bar makers also shave a curved hollow into the underside of each bar. This careful cut, called undercutting, tunes the bar so its note lands exactly where it should. Beneath the bars hang tubes called resonators, each one holding a column of air that vibrates along with the bar above it and swells the sound. The idea is very old. In West Africa, the balafon has been played for centuries, its wooden bars ringing over rows of dried gourds. In Southeast Asia, whole orchestras built around wooden and metal bars have existed for hundreds of years. The modern concert xylophone grew out of these older instruments, and today it sits at the bright, sharp end of the percussion section.

blocks.prompt: The Physics of a Wooden Note
blocks.text: At first glance a xylophone is nothing more than a row of wooden bars and a pair of mallets, but it is a small lesson in physics laid out in a straight line. Strike a bar and it flexes, bending down and springing back many times every second. Each of those springs shoves the surrounding air outward, and the ripples of pressure travel to your ear as a musical note. The speed of that flexing, measured in vibrations per second, is what we hear as pitch. Fast vibration sounds high, slow vibration sounds low. The genius of the instrument is that its shape controls its speed. A long bar carries more mass and bends more loosely, so it vibrates slowly and sounds a low note. A short bar is stiffer for its size and snaps back quickly, so it sounds a high note. This is why the bars are graded from long to short like a staircase of pitches. Makers fine tune each bar by carving a shallow arch into its underside. Removing wood from the middle lowers the note in a controlled way, letting a craftsman land each bar on an exact pitch rather than leaving it to chance. Two more features finish the design. Each bar is drilled and supported near the points where it naturally stays still while the rest of it vibrates, so the mounting does not deaden the sound. Below many bars hang tube resonators, columns of air tuned to match the bar above. When the bar sounds, the air column resonates in sympathy and makes the note fuller and longer. None of this is new. The xylophone belongs to a family of struck wooden instruments that stretches across the world and back through many centuries. The balafon of West Africa, with its gourd resonators, has been played for over seven hundred years and passed carefully from teacher to student. Tuned percussion built around wooden and metal bars anchors the gamelan orchestras of Indonesia. The bright concert xylophone that a modern player reads music from is a recent branch on a very old tree, and every one of its carefully cut bars still obeys the same plain physics: shorter and stiffer for high, longer and looser for low.

blocks.prompt: Wood, Air, and the Shape of a Note
blocks.text: A xylophone hides a surprising amount of physics inside a very plain shape. It is a set of tuned wooden bars struck with mallets, and it belongs to the class of instruments called idiophones, meaning the sound comes from the vibration of the instrument's own rigid body rather than from a string, a reed, or a stretched skin. Strike a bar and it does not simply buzz at one speed. It flexes in a whole pattern of bending waves, and along the bar there are quiet spots, called nodes, where the wood barely moves at all, and loud spots between them where it swings the most. Two facts about those bending waves shape everything a maker does. First, a longer, heavier bar bends more slowly than a short, stiff one, which is why pitch falls as the bars lengthen. Second, a struck bar does not produce a single clean tone. It vibrates in several patterns at once, each with its own frequency, and by default those extra frequencies are not musically related to the main one, so the raw note sounds clangy. This is where craft enters. By carving a shallow arch out of the underside of the bar, a maker thins the middle and lowers the main pitch, but more cleverly, the exact shape of that cut pulls the higher vibration patterns into tidy ratios above the fundamental, so the whole note rings as a musical pitch instead of a clatter. Mounting matters too. If you clamped a bar in the middle you would smother it, so bars are drilled and rested at their nodes, near a point about a fifth of the way in from each end, where the wood is naturally still. There the support holds the bar without draining its energy. Beneath the better instruments hang resonator tubes, each roughly a quarter of the sounding wavelength long and closed at the bottom, so the air inside is tuned to the bar above it. When the bar sings, that air column resonates in sympathy and pours the sound back out, richer and more sustained. The design is ancient and global, which is worth remembering when it is dismissed as a beginner's toy. In West Africa the balafon, a wooden bar instrument with gourd resonators, has been played for roughly eight centuries. One historic balafon, the Sosso Bala of Guinea, is treated as a cultural treasure and its tradition is recognized by the wider world as heritage worth protecting. Across the ocean in Indonesia, gamelan orchestras are built around families of tuned bars and have shaped an entire musical culture. It is worth noting one point of confusion: many so called toy xylophones have metal bars, which technically makes them glockenspiels, while a true xylophone uses wood, and its larger, mellower cousin the marimba uses wider wooden bars over long resonators. Different materials, different voices, the same simple, powerful idea. A row of carefully shaped bars, each one obeying the plain rule that longer and looser means low while shorter and stiffer means high, turns a tap into music.
